summary: The Space travel calculator turns the spaceship mass and the required fuel mass into time passed on Earth (Travel details). That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Space travel calculator work?
sections.html:
The Space travel calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports time passed on Earth (Travel details) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the destination, which exoplanet? and which Star Trek destination?); then you type in the spaceship mass, the required fuel mass (Travel details), the engine efficiency (Hidden variables) and the engine efficiency (Hidden variables).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Space travel calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Time passed on Earth=(1 ÷ 299792458) × the square root of (distance × (spaceship acceleration × distance + 179751035747363528) ÷ spaceship acceleration)
X1=the natural log of ((1 ÷ 299792458) × spaceship acceleration × time passed on Earth + (1 ÷ 299792458) × the square root of ((spaceship acceleration ^ 2) × (time passed on Earth ^ 2) + 89875517873681764))
X1=(1 ÷ 299792458) × spaceship acceleration × time passed in spaceship
Time passed on Earth=(1 ÷ 299792458) × the square root of ((spaceship acceleration × distance + 89875517873681764 ^ 2) − 8077608713062490229263800746151696) ÷ spaceship acceleration
Maximum velocity=299792458 × spaceship acceleration × time passed on Earth ÷ the square root of ((spaceship acceleration ^ 2) × (time passed on Earth ^ 2) + 89875517873681764)
Maximum velocity=299792458 × β [v ÷ c]

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Acceleration, opening in gravitational acc. on Earth
  • Mass, opening in metric tons
  • Length, opening in light years
  • Length, opening in light years
  • Length, opening in light years
  • Time, opening in years
  • Time, opening in years
  • Mass, opening in metric tons

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Space travel calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the spaceship mass and the required fuel mass — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Space travel calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns time passed on Earth (Travel details), derived from the spaceship mass and the required fuel mass. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Space travel calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the spaceship mass and the required fuel mass, which is 12 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter spaceship acceleration in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Spaceship acceleration opens in gravitational acc. on Earth and the chip beside it offers 5 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (6 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Distance = 0 ly. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Space travel calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
